t: Aristocracy, Greek for “rule of the best”, was praised by Plato and Aristotle as government by the most virtuous, but in practice it almost always meant rule by a hereditary, landowning nobility.
Noble elites governed most of Europe and much of Asia for over two thousand years, through bodies as varied as the Roman Senate, Venice’s Great Council, the Polish Sejm and Britain’s House of Lords.
Revolutions, new commercial and industrial wealth, mass democracy and the First World War stripped aristocracies of their power; only remnants, such as the noble seats in Tonga’s parliament, survive.
dyk: From 1652 a single deputy in the Sejm of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth could end a session and void all it had passed by declaring “I do not allow”; this noble privilege, the liberum veto, was abolished only in 1791.
ev: The Bacchiad clan replaces the kings of Corinth with a magistrate chosen yearly from among its own members
By Roman tradition the last king is expelled, and patrician families rule through the Senate and two annual consuls
Aristotle’s Politics defines aristocracy as rule by the best for the common good and oligarchy as its corruption
Fujiwara no Michinaga becomes regent for his grandson Emperor Go-Ichijō, the height of Fujiwara power in Japan
The Polish–Lithuanian nobility holds its first free royal election and binds the new king by the Henrician Articles
On 4 August France’s National Assembly abolishes noble privileges; hereditary nobility itself is abolished in 1790
The Parliament Act ends the House of Lords’ power to veto bills passed by the House of Commons
Revolution topples the German and Austrian monarchies, sweeping away noble chambers such as the Prussian House of Lords

f.power: A small hereditary or landed elite, acting through councils, senates, diets and upper houses, often beside a monarch who depended on it
f.legitimacy: A claim to excellence of birth, virtue and education, upheld by landed wealth, military service, custom and royal grants of title
f.chosen: Membership passes by birth and is guarded by intermarriage; monarchs ennoble newcomers, and councils co-opt or elect their members from the privileged families
f.examples: Corinth under the Bacchiadae, the Roman Republic, Heian Japan under the Fujiwara regents, the Republic of Venice, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, Great Britain in the 18th century
